sheet.line: Bay Scallop Crudo: Meyer Lemon, Black Tru[ffle], Radish (cut at the page edge; read as Black Truffle, asked in tg-menu)

facts.text: Bay scallops are the small scallops of shallow estuaries and bays, about an inch across and roughly 50 to 90 to the pound, against sea scallops of about two inches from deeper water at 10 to 20 to the pound; bay scallops are the sweeter and more tender, sea scallops chewier. The sources disagree on the season.

Under the FDA Food Code a scallop product made only of the shucked adductor muscle is exempt from parasite destruction by freezing, as oysters, clams and mussels are; most other fish served raw must be frozen first. The consumer advisory for raw animal foods still applies.

The Meyer lemon was collected near Peking (Beijing) in 1908 by Frank N. Meyer, a USDA plant explorer, and introduced to the United States as S.P.I. 23028. It is deep yellow with an orange tint when ripe, thin skinned, sweeter and less acidic than a common lemon. Long called a lemon and mandarin cross, it is now thought to be a cross of citron, mandarin and pummelo.

The black Perigord truffle, Tuber melanosporum, is a winter truffle, harvested from mid-November to mid-March (December to February in some Spanish studies), prized for its aroma; the brumale truffle grows in the same soils and is often confused with it.

A radish's bite is made when it is cut or chewed: glucosinolates and the enzyme myrosinase, stored apart in the cells, meet and form isothiocyanates, the mustard oils of the mustard family (mustard, horseradish, wasabi).
